snippets.snippet_text: The Hebrew word massa ('oracle') derives from nasa', meaning 'to lift' or 'to carry'—a prophetic revelation is literally a burden the prophet bears, not merely poetic metaphor. This double meaning opens Isaiah's entire series of foreign-nation pronouncements.

God calls the armies summoned to destroy Babylon His 'sanctified ones' (mequddashim)—set apart for sacred use in executing divine judgment. Yet these nations act without knowing they serve God's purposes, revealing that all earthly power ultimately serves the Lord's will, whether acknowledged or not.

When Isaiah declares the stars will 'withdraw their shining' during the Day of the LORD, he reverses creation itself. In Hebrew thought, stars were tokens of God's covenant permanence (Genesis 15:5); to extinguish them unmakes the fundamental promise of order and redemption.

Isaiah 14:12-14 contains Scripture's most detailed exposition of human pride: five consecutive 'I will' declarations of cosmic usurpation. The fallen king claims 'I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the most High'—the exact ambition that defines rebellion against God in temple theology.

Jerusalem's leaders respond to siege not with repentance but by engineering solutions: surveying walls, rationing water, even demolishing homes for materials. God's rebuke cuts deeper: they made a ditch without 'looking unto the maker thereof'—a stunning indictment of self-reliance masquerading as competence.

Isaiah 22:22 gives Eliakim the 'key of the house of David'—authority to 'open' and 'shut,' determining who enters the Lord's house. Christ quotes this verse verbatim (Revelation 3:7), applying it to His own redemptive authority, making the stewardship of sacred keys a Christological type.
